chapter: New Orleans lineage and brass bands
title: Who owns the music: generations of New Orleans players and brass bands
summary: Asked about American versus German jazz, Armstrong says no one can say who copied whom, traces the lineage Merritt, Buddy Bolden, Oliver, and recalls brass band parades and second liners.

story.theme_name: Brass bands, parades and jazz funerals
story.community_name: Parading for Mardi Gras and the clubs

blocks.x: Do you think there are different kinds of jazz? He said he spoke about American jazz with his friends and German jazz.

Well, we don't look at it that way. I mean, when I play with them boys, they sound the same as anybody over here. I'm just saying that. And then... You mean the copy? How do we know who copy? Who we... Who, how... For generations, before my time was Joe Oliver. I was mine. Of course, there was other good ones, but I'm just narrating it down. And before Joe Oliver's time was Buddy Baldwin. Before Buddy Baldwin was an old man, so-and-so way back then, probably old man Merritt. That's generations. Now, how we know who owns it? So if it comes out alright, don't worry who wrote it. Well, as long as it sounds good, listen. Okay, what it is? You don't name where we come from. If we play in a brass band, we play March. We play the same tempo that big swing orchestra, you know, that bass drum beater. Who didn't he ramble, you know? Boom, jam, that's jam. And that's when the, the, the, the members of the art fellows just parading. Then the guys from the pool room or somewhere, they, they, they think they're just as proud as the fellows in the parade. What happened here? You remember June Panama? Well, Joe Oliver, now I'm just a kid, your age. But I didn't want to go with the other children, go up to the other schools and fight, and like the rock and rollers think they should do. That's what taught the music, because the music comes from the sanctified churches, and we always appreciate it. But they give it the name rock and roll, and, and we listen. That's why we can remember what we heard. But we didn't fight and pull up seats, and the other guy trying to be straight, but he's scared. They call him a sissy or something less what you get when they fight like that. But, uh, I remember when the Arnold Brass Band was playing in the Labor Day parade, and you got fifteen bands, and, uh, all these bands had to open up for Joe Oliver and his brass band to come in. You know, that bass hook, they, on the side, beat the, and the, what we call the second liners, the, the, the, the guys with the shirt sleeves, that from the pool rooms and things.
